🚨🚨BREAKING UPDATES 🚨 

🇵🇭 Death Toll Climbs to 11 in Philippines Landfill Disaster
Cebu City, Philippines 

A tragic collapse at a large landfill in Cebu City has now claimed 11 lives, with more than 20 people still missing. The incident happened at the Binaliw landfill, where heavy rain in recent weeks made the piles of trash unstable and heavier, leading to the slide.

Rescue teams have been working hard but hopes of finding more survivors are fading after three days. They have already saved 12 injured people from the rubble. A local fire official said it's unlikely anyone else is still alive under the debris.

The government has stepped in quickly. The company running the landfill, Prime Integrated Waste Solutions, has been told to stop operations and fix any issues within 90 days. Officials will investigate what went wrong and hold those responsible accountable.

Lawmakers are calling for big changes to how the country handles waste, including better safety for workers at these sites. This isn't the first time something like this has happened in the Philippines, where big cities like Cebu rely on huge landfills for trash.

People on social media are sharing sadness and anger, with some blaming poor management. Experts say better rules and checks could prevent future tragedies. Updates are expected as the search continues.

Source: BBC World

🚨🚨BREAKING UPDATES 🚨 

🇵🇭Signs of Life Found in Deadly Rubbish Collapse at Philippine Landfill

A massive pile of garbage suddenly collapsed at a waste facility in Binaliw village, Cebu City, in the central Philippines, on January 8, 2026. The avalanche buried workers and buildings, killing at least four people, including an engineer and an office worker. Rescuers have pulled out 12 injured survivors so far, but 36 others are still missing.

On January 10, officials said they detected signs of life in the debris, giving hope for more rescues. Teams of police, firefighters, and disaster workers are carefully digging through the twisted metal and trash, using a big 50-ton crane to help. They must be extra careful because the area is unstable and there could be dangerous gases.

The cause isn't fully known yet, but heavy rains from a recent typhoon and an earthquake last year might have made the ground weak. Cebu City, a busy port with about a million people, now faces a garbage buildup problem as the site is closed.

This isn't the first time—landfills in the Philippines have been risky for years, especially near poor areas where people look for food and items in the trash. In 2000, a similar collapse near Manila killed over 200 people. One survivor from this event, Jaylord Antigua, called it traumatic and said it felt like the end until he escaped. Rescue efforts continue as families wait for news.

Source: Sky News
